title: Clustering
content:
Clustering is an \textbf{unsupervised learning} task in which examples are grouped into clusters based purely on how similar or close they are to one another, without using any class labels. Unlike classification, the algorithm is never told the correct group for any example; it must discover the natural groupings on its own using distance or similarity.

This is the opposite setting from Naive Bayes or Decision Trees, where every training example came with a known class label attached.

Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering
content: Agglomerative clustering builds a hierarchy of clusters bottom-up: it starts with every point as its own cluster, and repeatedly merges the two closest clusters (using a chosen linkage rule) until only one cluster remains. The resulting merge history is displayed as a tree diagram called a \textbf{dendrogram}, where the height of each merge shows the distance at which it happened.

title: Agglomerative Clustering Algorithm
content:
\textbf{Input:} a set of $n$ points, a linkage method (single, complete, or average)

\textbf{Output:} a dendrogram showing the full merge history

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item Start with $n$ clusters, one for each point.
\item Compute the pairwise distance between every pair of clusters.
\item Find the two clusters with the smallest distance and merge them into one cluster.
\item Record the distance at which this merge happened (this becomes a height on the dendrogram).
\item Recompute the distance from the newly merged cluster to every remaining cluster using the chosen linkage rule.
\item Repeat steps 3 to 5 until only one cluster remains.
\item Return the full sequence of merges as a dendrogram.
\end{enumerate}

Reading a Dendrogram and Comparing Linkages:
content:
\textbf{Reading a Dendrogram and Comparing Linkages:}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item The \textbf{height} of a merge shows how far apart the two clusters were when they joined; lower merges happened first
\item Cutting the dendrogram at any height gives a clustering: cut low for many small clusters, cut high for fewer large clusters
\item \textbf{Single linkage} can produce long chained clusters since it only needs one close pair
\item \textbf{Complete linkage} produces tighter, more compact clusters since it is controlled by the farthest pair
\item \textbf{Average linkage} balances between the two, using the mean of all cross-cluster distances
\end{enumerate}

title: k-Means Clustering
content: k-Means is a \textbf{partitional} clustering algorithm that divides $n$ points into exactly $k$ clusters, where $k$ is chosen in advance. Each cluster is represented by its \textbf{centroid} (the mean position of all points currently in that cluster), and every point is assigned to the cluster whose centroid is nearest to it.

title: Properties of k-Means
k-Means Algorithm (Lloyd's Algorithm)
content:
\textbf{Input:} a set of $n$ points, the number of clusters $k$, initial centroids $c_1,\ldots,c_k$

\textbf{Output:} $k$ clusters with their final centroids

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item Choose $k$ initial centroids (often $k$ of the data points themselves).
\item Assign every point to the cluster whose centroid is nearest, using Euclidean distance.
\item Recompute each centroid as the mean of all points currently assigned to that cluster.
\item If any point changed cluster in step 2, or any centroid moved in step 3, go back to step 2.
\item Otherwise (no reassignment and no centroid movement) stop; the clustering has converged.
\item Return the final clusters and centroids.
\end{enumerate}

Sum of Squared Errors (SSE)
content:
The Sum of Squared Errors measures how tightly the points fit their assigned clusters:
\[
SSE = \sum_{j=1}^{k}\sum_{x \in \text{Cluster}_j} d(x,c_j)^2
\]
where $c_j$ is the centroid of Cluster $j$. A \textbf{lower} SSE means the points are, on average, closer to their own cluster's centroid — a tighter, better clustering.

This is simply the squared-distance idea from Section 3.1.2, summed over every point in every cluster.

The Elbow Method for Choosing k:
content:
\textbf{The Elbow Method for Choosing k:}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item SSE always \textbf{decreases} as $k$ increases (more clusters means points sit closer to their centroids), reaching $SSE=0$ when $k=n$
\item Plot SSE against $k$: the curve drops sharply at first, then flattens out
\item The \textbf{elbow point} — where the drop suddenly slows down, as at $k=2$ in Example 3.18 — is chosen as a good balance between simplicity (few clusters) and tightness (low SSE)
\item Choosing $k$ too large just to minimize SSE defeats the purpose of clustering, since $k=n$ trivially gives $SSE=0$ with every point in its own cluster
\end{enumerate}

title: Self-Organizing Map (SOM)
Best Matching Unit (BMU)
content:
For a given input vector $x$, the Best Matching Unit is the neuron whose weight vector $w_j$ is closest to $x$ (using Euclidean distance):
\[
\text{BMU} = \arg\min_j \; d(x, w_j)
\]

title: SOM Weight Update Rule
content:
After finding the BMU for input $x$, every neuron $j$ within the BMU's neighbourhood updates its weight vector to move slightly closer to $x$:
\[
w_j^{\text{new}} = w_j^{\text{old}} + \eta \cdot \left(x - w_j^{\text{old}}\right)
\]
where $\eta$ is the learning rate ($0<\eta\le1$). Neurons outside the neighbourhood are left unchanged.

This update rule is just "move a fraction $\eta$ of the way from the old weight toward the input" — the same kind of small-step adjustment used in gradient-based learning.

title: Self-Organizing Map Training (Simplified)
content:
\textbf{Input:} training points, a grid of neurons with initial weight vectors, learning rate $\eta$, neighbourhood radius $r$

\textbf{Output:} trained neuron weight vectors

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item Pick a training input $x$.
\item Compute the distance from $x$ to every neuron's weight vector and find the BMU (smallest distance).
\item Identify all neurons within radius $r$ of the BMU on the grid (the neighbourhood).
\item Update the weight vector of the BMU and every neuron in its neighbourhood using $w_j^{\text{new}} = w_j^{\text{old}} + \eta(x-w_j^{\text{old}})$.
\item Repeat steps 1 to 4 for every training input (one full pass is called an epoch).
\item Optionally shrink $\eta$ and $r$ slightly and repeat for more epochs.
\item Return the final weight vectors.
\end{enumerate}

SOM vs k-Means: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] Both find
content:
\textbf{SOM vs k-Means:}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item Both find a "closest representative vector" for each input, exactly like a BMU (SOM) or nearest centroid (k-Means)
\item k-Means updates \textbf{only} the winning centroid; SOM updates the winning neuron \textbf{and} its grid neighbours, which is what creates the topology-preserving map
\item In SOM, neurons that are close on the grid end up with similar weight vectors after training, so the map can be visualized to show which regions of input space are related
\item A larger learning rate $\eta$ makes each update move the weight vector further toward the input, exactly as seen by comparing the update sizes in Examples 3.20 and 3.21
\end{enumerate}

title: k-Nearest Neighbor (k-NN)
k-Nearest Neighbor Algorithm
content:
\textbf{Input:} training points with known class labels, a test point $q$, the number of neighbors $k$

\textbf{Output:} predicted class label for $q$

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item Compute the distance from $q$ to every training point.
\item Sort the training points by distance to $q$ in increasing order.
\item Select the $k$ closest training points (the $k$ nearest neighbors).
\item Count how many of these $k$ neighbors belong to each class.
\item Assign $q$ the class that appears most often among the $k$ neighbors (majority vote).
\item Return the predicted class.
\end{enumerate}

Example 3.24 --- Classifying with a Tie Broken by Closer Points
Choosing k in k-NN: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] A
content:
\textbf{Choosing k in k-NN:}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item A \textbf{small} $k$ (e.g. $k=1$) is sensitive to noise — one mislabeled nearby point can flip the prediction
\item A \textbf{large} $k$ smooths out noise but risks pulling in points from a different, more distant class
\item $k$ is usually chosen \textbf{odd} for two-class problems specifically to avoid ties, as seen in Example 3.24
\item k-NN needs no explicit training phase, but classifying each new point requires computing its distance to \textbf{every} training point, which is why it is called "lazy" learning
\end{enumerate}

title: Example 3.25 --- Effect of Increasing k
content:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{cccc}
\toprule
Point & $x_1$ & $x_2$ & Class \\
\midrule
$P_1$ & 1 & 1 & A \\
$P_2$ & 2 & 1 & A \\
$P_3$ & 2 & 3 & B \\
$P_4$ & 8 & 8 & B \\
$P_5$ & 9 & 9 & B \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Classify $q=(2,2)$ using k-NN with (a) $k=1$ and (b) $k=3$, and compare the results.

\textbf{Solution:}
\begin{align*}
d(q,P_1) &= \sqrt{1+1} \approx 1.414 \\
d(q,P_2) &= \sqrt{0+1} = 1 \\
d(q,P_3) &= \sqrt{0+1} = 1 \\
d(q,P_4) &= \sqrt{36+36} \approx 8.485 \\
d(q,P_5) &= \sqrt{49+49} \approx 9.899
\end{align*}
\textbf{(a) $k=1$:} There is a tie for nearest between $P_2$ (distance 1, class A) and $P_3$ (distance 1, class B); assuming $P_2$ is selected first, the prediction is A.
\textbf{(b) $k=3$:} The 3 nearest neighbors are $P_2(A)$, $P_3(B)$, $P_1(A)$ — majority is 2 A's vs 1 B.
\boxed{k=1 \Rightarrow A \text{ (tie-sensitive)}, \qquad k=3 \Rightarrow A \text{ (clear majority)}}
Here both choices happen to agree, but $k=3$ reaches its answer through a clear majority vote rather than a distance tie, making it the more robust choice.
